claim_checks.claim: Fowler's catalog records “Replace Conditional with Polymorphism” as the refactoring that moves per-variant behavior behind polymorphic operations.
claim_checks.page_says: switch (bird.type) { case 'EuropeanSwallow': return “average”; ... class EuropeanSwallow { get plumage() { return “average”;
claim_checks.note: The catalog entry titled Replace Conditional with Polymorphism shows a switch over bird.type replaced by one class per type, each with its own plumage getter: per-variant behavior moved into polymorphic methods. The preceding sentence of the paragraph carries no mark and was not graded.

claim_checks.claim: Subtype polymorphism lets a value of a more specific type be used through a shared supertype, interface, trait object, or protocol.
claim_checks.page_says: not found: searched 'polymorph', 'subtype', 'supertype', 'protocol', 'interface'. Closest: "We can use trait objects in place of a generic or concrete type."
claim_checks.note: The Rust trait-objects chapter never defines subtype polymorphism, supertypes, interfaces or protocols; it only shows values of different types implementing one trait used through a trait object, and likens that to duck typing. The general definition and the term are unsourced.

claim_checks.claim: Parametric polymorphism uses type parameters so one implementation can work for many types while preserving type information, as TypeScript generics and Rust trait bounds do.
claim_checks.page_says: this version of the identity function is generic, as it works over a range of types. Unlike using any, it’s also just as precise
claim_checks.note: The TypeScript part is supported by the generics page. The Rust trait bounds part is not in [^2] (it is in [^6], which this claim does not cite), and the term 'parametric polymorphism' does not appear on the cited pages (searched 'polymorph', 'parametric').

claim_checks.claim: Ad-hoc polymorphism gives the same operation name multiple implementations, such as TypeScript overload signatures or Rust traits implemented for different types.
claim_checks.page_says: write some number of function signatures (usually two or more), followed by the body of the function ... Then, we wrote a function implementation with a compatible signature.
claim_checks.note: TypeScript overloads give one function several call signatures backed by a single implementation, the opposite of 'multiple implementations'. The Rust part is not in [^2] at all, and 'ad-hoc polymorphism' is not on the cited pages (searched 'polymorph', 'ad-hoc', 'ad hoc'). The rank 1 TypeScript page governs; recorded here as a grounding finding rather than a separate KB-17 conflict.

claim_checks.claim: Dynamic dispatch selects a method implementation at runtime when the compiler cannot know the concrete receiver type; Rust trait objects use dynamic dispatch for this case.
claim_checks.page_says: _dynamic dispatch_, which is when the compiler can’t tell at compile time which method you’re calling ... When we use trait objects, Rust must use dynamic dispatch.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript type compatibility is structural: a value is compatible when it has the target type's required members, unlike nominal systems that require explicit declarations.
claim_checks.page_says: The basic rule for TypeScript’s structural type system is that x is compatible with y if y has at least the same members as x.
claim_checks.note: Structural vs nominal is supported. The page states the member rule as 'the basic rule' with exceptions (private/protected members; 'object literals may only specify known properties'); the claim drops that qualifier and says 'required members', a word the page does not use.

claim_checks.claim: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly by any type whose method set matches the interface, so a type does not announce the relationship in its declaration.
claim_checks.page_says: The type set defined by such an interface is the set of types which implement all of those methods ... called basic interfaces.
claim_checks.note: The spec ties method-set satisfaction to basic interfaces; general interfaces with type terms (~T, unions) define type sets beyond method sets, so 'Go interfaces' is wider than the page. 'Implicitly' and 'does not announce' are not stated but follow from the spec defining implementation purely as type-set membership 'regardless of what other methods S1 and S2 may have'.

claim_checks.claim: Rust traits define shared behavior and trait bounds constrain generic parameters to types that provide that behavior.
claim_checks.page_says: We can use traits to define shared behavior ... We can use _trait bounds_ to specify that a generic type can be any type that has certain behavior.

claim_checks.claim: Wadler's expression problem frames a trade-off: functional data variants make it easy to add new functions, while OO subclasses make it easy to add new variants.
claim_checks.page_says: In a functional language, the rows are fixed ... it is easy to add new columns (functions). In an object-oriented language ... it is easy to add new rows (subclasses).
claim_checks.note: Grounded, but [^7] is rank 6 and sits in role 3, which allows ranks 1-4: KB-15 breach recorded separately.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript uses narrowing and `never` checks to support exhaustive handling.
claim_checks.page_says: This means you can use narrowing and rely on never turning up to do exhaustive checking in a switch statement.
claim_checks.note: The preceding sentence ('A discriminated union with an exhaustive switch is better when ...') carries no mark, is not supported by [^8], and is trade-off advice in a role 3 section (see structure violation).

claim_checks.claim: YAGNI avoids speculative subclasses before a second variant.
claim_checks.page_says: not found: searched 'yagni', 'speculative', 'one variant', 'second variant' in Wadler's note.
claim_checks.note: Checked because it cites a rank 6 source. Wadler's note is about adding cases and functions without recompiling; it says nothing about YAGNI or single-variant designs.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript can narrow branches and detect unhandled `never` cases.
claim_checks.page_says: rely on never turning up to do exhaustive checking in a switch statement. ... Adding a new member to the Shape union, will cause a TypeScript error

claim_checks.claim: Callers can add new implementations without editing the central package.
claim_checks.page_says: When we wrote the library, we didn’t know that someone might add the `SelectBox` type, but our `Screen` implementation was able to operate on the new type
claim_checks.note: Listing 18-8 is 'Another crate using `gui` and implementing the `Draw` trait'. The row's 'interface' option is context only; the page covers trait objects.

claim_checks.page_says: if the target type contains a private member, then the source type must also contain a private member that originated from the same class.

claim_checks.claim: Generics are monomorphized; trait objects use runtime dispatch.
claim_checks.page_says: using generics and trait bounds is preferable because the definitions will be monomorphized at compile time ... When we use trait objects, Rust must use dynamic dispatch.
claim_checks.note: The row's 'homogeneous list, prefer generics' context matches the page's 'If you’ll only ever have homogeneous collections'.

violations.evidence: C9 cites [^7], a rank 6 mailing-list email, in a role 3 section that allows ranks 1-4.
C2 unsupported: [^5] never defines subtype polymorphism, supertypes, interfaces or protocols.
C3 unsupported: the Rust trait bounds part is not in the cited [^2] (only in uncited [^6]); the term 'parametric polymorphism' is on no cited page.
C4 contradicted: [^2] says TypeScript overloads are several signatures 'followed by the body of the function' (one implementation), not multiple implementations; the Rust part is not in [^2].
C6 overstates: page states 'the basic rule' with exceptions (private/protected members, object-literal known properties); claim drops the qualifier and adds 'required members'.
C7 overstates: method-set satisfaction is stated for basic interfaces; claim widens it to all Go interfaces.
E1 unsupported: Wadler's note [^7] says nothing about YAGNI or single-variant designs.

The section mixes concept-architecture definitions (kinds of polymorphism), mechanism (dispatch, structural typing) and trade-off advice ('A discriminated union with an exhaustive switch is better when ...', the expression problem framing), which belong in roles 2 and 6.
Shows a before/after refactoring but no run: no call with real inputs and the outputs it returns.
No section holds role 2 (concept architecture) or role 5 (reference & invariants); Takeaways restates How it works and Edge cases.
